name: Carbuncle
lede: Carbuncle is the old name of the red gem that medieval writers said glowed in the dark, taken from the Latin for a small coal; as a color word it now labels a very dark reddish brown.

sections.title: A little coal
sections.body:
*Carbuncle* comes from the Latin *carbunculus*, a small burning coal [1][2]. It shares that root with *carbon*, and the gem earned the name because it seemed to be on fire [1]. In Shakespeare's time English speakers called rubies carbuncles, and the Greeks had called the same stones *anthrax*, which also means coal [1]. French kept the older form, *escarboucle*, the carbuncle of knights and poets [2].

The fire metaphor had a less flattering second life. The word was later extended to a boil, so that the name of a jewel became the name of an infection [1]. Birren reports that an Arab physician prescribed powdered amber against boils, carbuncles and ulcers [8].

sections.title: The swatch is not the stone
sections.body:
The color on this page is a very dark red-brown, #462621, taken from Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color* of 1930 [10]. That book dates the color name to 1634 and places it on plate 8 [10]. Two other names from the same book, London Brown (first recorded 1806) and Andorra (1927), are near-duplicates of it in our library [10].

Nothing about this color is fiery. Its nearest neighbors in our library are [[mahogany]], about ten units away, and [[dusty-oxblood]] [10]. Our name tables also file Carbuncle among the alternate names of [[chocolate-brown]] [10]. Why a dark brown carries a gem's name is undocumented in the books we hold.

sections.title: The stone that shone in the dark
sections.body:
In the thirteenth century European writers made the carbuncle the highest of all gems [3]. Thomas of Cantimpré, writing in the first quarter of the century, called it by far the most important stone because it could turn night into day [3]. He ranked even its poorest grade, the balas ruby, above the sapphire and the jasper [3].

Albertus Magnus gave the fullest reasoning in his *Book of Minerals*, written about 1230 [3]. Citing Hermetic writings, he said that stones carry the colors of the heavens: the sapphire the color of the starless sphere, a bright white the color of most stars, and a fiery, flashing color the sun and Mars [3]. That last color, he held, belonged above all to the carbuncle, which was therefore the noblest stone, as gold is among metals [3]. A good one, he wrote, shone in the dark like a live coal, and he said he had seen such a stone himself [3]. Gage reads this as a move from the primacy of the sapphire to the primacy of the carbuncle, part of a wider habit of valuing stones by the light they carried [3].

The shift explains an earlier confession. In the 1140s Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis wrote that the Cross of Saint Eloy and the Escrin de Charlemagne held all nine stones of Ezekiel's Eden, apart from the carbuncle [3]. Gage reads his frankness as knowledge that a true carbuncle shone in the dark, and doubt that the red stones in his treasures did [3]. Ambrogio Lorenzetti, by Gage's account, coded the virtues in his Good Government fresco of 1338 to 1339 with blue, green, diamond and carbuncle, colors taken from a recent exposition of the meanings of gems [4].

sections.title: Lips, shields and the Grail
sections.body:
In the romances and poems of the Middle Ages the *escarboucle* was a ruby of unusual cut or special brilliance [2]. Poets compared a small, plump, bright red mouth to it, and some rhymed *boche*, an old form of *bouche* (mouth), with *escarboche* [2]. Others set an escarboucle at the center of a shield or on the helmet of a virtuous knight [2].

The stone was believed to glow like burning coals, to guide the knight through the dark and to protect him from evil [2]. Bestiaries added that dragons carried a similar stone behind the forehead, and that winning it was a rewarded exploit [2]. The Grail glowed in the same way, casting a red, white and golden light [2]. Chrétien de Troyes introduced it in an unfinished romance of about the 1180s, and authors afterward disagreed on whether it was a dish, a chalice, a cauldron or a stone [2]. Wolfram von Eschenbach chose the stone [2].

sections.title: Which stone did the Bible mean?
sections.body:
The word sits in English Bibles [5][6]. Ezekiel's Eden is covered in every precious stone, among them the sardius, topaz, diamond, onyx, jasper, sapphire, emerald and carbuncle, a verse Aldous Huxley used to argue that heaven is always a place of gems [5]. In the older translation Finlay quotes for the priest's breastplate, the first row holds a sardius, a topaz and a carbuncle [6]. The newer translation she quotes first has a sard, a topaz and an emerald in the same place [6].

Finlay's table of Hebrew stone names does not use the word carbuncle, and offers amethyst or emerald for *Bereketh*, the entry that fits the third stone of that row [6]. The carbuncle of the older Bible is therefore a translator's choice more than an identification [6].

sections.title: Books disagree
sections.body:
Books disagree on what a carbuncle was. Finlay treats it as an old English name for the ruby [1]. Pastoureau says a ruby was called an escarboucle only when it was unusually cut or shone with particular brilliance [2]. Gage's medieval sources count the balas ruby as the lowest grade of carbuncle [3], and our gem notes identify the balas ruby as a spinel [11].

The safest reading is that *carbuncle* named a quality and a legend, the red stone that burned from within, more than any one mineral. Its likeliest bodies were [[gem:ruby|ruby]] and [[gem:spinel|spinel]], with red [[gem:garnet|garnet]] in the wings [11].

sections.title: A measure of red
sections.body: The word stayed in use as a yardstick of depth in red. In 1873 Charles Reade wrote to the *Pall Mall Gazette* about Stradivari's varnish, which he thought ended with a coat of mastic and dragon's blood [7]. He described the best lumps of that resin as deeper in color than a carbuncle [7]. Arthur Conan Doyle later put the word in the title of a Sherlock Holmes story, "The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle", where it can only mean a gem, not a red one [9].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 2,232 works, or 9.4 per cent [12]. It is a common painted color, though not a bright one. The match rate is highest in the 1500s, at 16 per cent (356 of 2,231 paintings), and lowest in the 1900s, at 5.8 per cent (97 of 1,674) [12]. The peak decade is the 1530s, when 39 of 178 paintings match, 2.3 times the archive-wide rate [12]. The earliest match is a Virgin and Child enthroned of about 1210, where it covers 24 per cent of the panel [12].

[[painter:bronzino|Bronzino]] has 9 matching paintings out of 21 in the archive, and [[painter:pontormo|Pontormo]] 6 out of 13 [12]. The widest matches are Min Zhen's [[painting:cma-152821|album of 1788]], at 84 per cent of the image, and Pieter de Hooch's [[painting:commons-Q20003837|Soldier Offering a Woman a Glass of Wine]], of 1650, at 73 per cent [12].

The most telling number is where the color sits. In the paintings that contain it, it falls in the shadows 68 times in 100 and in the mid-tones 32 times, never in the highlights [12]. The color that medieval writers called the stone's fire is, in paint, the color of shadow. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a screen color, not a pigment test [12].

questions.q: Why did Abbot Suger admit his treasures lacked a carbuncle?
choices: A true carbuncle was believed to shine in the dark, and he could not vouch that his red stones did
Carbuncles were illegal to own in France
The stone had not yet been discovered
He thought red stones were unlucky
questions.answer: A true carbuncle was believed to shine in the dark, and he could not vouch that his red stones did

questions.q: True or false: the Carbuncle swatch on this page is a bright, glowing red.
What does the Latin root of carbuncle mean?

openers: The stone medieval writers ranked above the sapphire because it supposedly glowed in the dark is, as a color name today, a very dark brown.
In paintings the carbuncle swatch lives in the shadows: 68 times in 100, never in the highlights.
Carbuncle and anthrax are the Latin and Greek words for the same thing: a glowing coal that English once used for the ruby.
